  The newest chapter is the kernel-to-userspace
  boundary: QUIC reimplements congestion control in
  userspace, letting applications like BBR or CUBIC
  with new loss detection ship independently of OS
  kernels, and IEEE 802.11's aggregation and 5G's
  buffer behavior keep producing tailored variants
  like BBRv2, Copa, and Swift.

  DONE

❯ Without using any tools, think it through, then
  write about 700 words on how TCP congestion control
  evolved. End with DONE.

✻ Thought for 1 second [ctrl+o to expand]

⠶ Early TCP had no notion of congestion at all. The
  protocol treated a lost packet as evidence of a
  transmission error on a link, retransmitted it, and
  moved on. On the small, lightly loaded networks of
  the early 1980s that was tolerable. On the rapidly
  growing internet it was catastrophic. In October 1986
   the link between Lawrence Berkeley Lab and UC
  Berkeley collapsed from 32 Kbps to roughly 40 bps — a
   thousandfold drop — and the mechanism was clear
  after the fact: overload caused buffer overflow and
  drops, drops caused aggressive timer-based
  retransmissions, and those retransmissions deepened
  the overload. The network could saturate itself with
  duplicate traffic while delivering almost nothing.

  Van Jacobson's 1988 paper "Congestion Avoidance and
  Control" reframed loss on a wired network as a
  congestion signal, and introduced the algorithms —

 ☆ Resolving…  119
